messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos, a 24‑year‑old financial analyst of Puerto Rican descent, lives alone in a small apartment in the city. Two years ago, while deployed in Afghanistan, he witnessed the sudden death of a close comrade during an ambush. The sound of a sudden explosion, the metallic taste of blood, and the frantic scramble for cover were imprinted so vividly that the memory still flashes before his eyes in a rush of clarity. He remembers the exact scent of burning plastic, the frantic voice of a wounded soldier, and the brief, disorienting pause when the firefight ended. The loss left him feeling utterly bereft; the future seemed a blank canvas, and his sense of self was irrevocably altered. The traumatic flashbacks have carved a path from Carlos’s internal sense of hopelessness to the way he recalls the battle. Because he believes his future is doomed and that he has become a permanent outsider, the images from that day refuse to settle into a coherent narrative. Instead, they erupt as sudden, isolated fragments that swirl in his mind, each fragment a stark reminder that the past is trapped in a looping, unchangeable sequence. The feeling that nothing he does will matter only amplifies the vividness of these memories, and the confusion in their order makes each recollection feel more immediate and destabilizing. These vivid, confusing memories, in turn, trigger Carlos’s avoidance behaviors. When a sudden piece of the past surfaces—perhaps the clatter of a distant office printer echoing like artillery—he instinctively retreats. The open, sunlit lobby of his workplace feels exposed and unsafe; the open‑plan office where colleagues converse freely feels like a battlefield. The very act of speaking about the incident, even in a casual chat with a coworker, feels like revisiting the battlefield, so he stops engaging in those conversations. The memories’ suddenness and intensity make him feel that confronting them will reopen wounds he thought were buried. Carlos’s deep‑rooted negative appraisals also reinforce these maladaptive strategies. His belief that he has no future compels him to withdraw from social interactions and avoid anything that might force him to face the grief of his fallen friend. The conviction that he has violated his own values—by surviving when others did not—makes him feel that sharing his experience would expose his own perceived failure. The outsider label he carries—viewing himself as permanently detached from the normal life of colleagues—further fuels his reluctance to participate in team meetings or to spend time in the open spaces of the office where he feels most vulnerable. These loops of avoidance have begun to erode his professional life. Carlos has missed several key presentations because the mere thought of speaking in the open forum sends a wave of panic, and he has avoided the open stairwell in the building, insisting on walking a longer, more circuitous route that wastes valuable time. He has begun to resent the fluorescent lighting of his cubicle, which he believes mocks his internal darkness. His supervisor has noted a decline in his punctuality and a subtle withdrawal from collaborative projects, attributing it to “personal reasons” that the analyst has never clarified. The cumulative toll of these behaviors has left Carlos feeling isolated and stuck. He finally decided to seek therapy after a brief but intense panic attack during a client call, where the ringing of the phone and the sudden burst of the client’s voice triggered a flashback that made him physically ill. What he fears most is that he will never be able to re‑engage with his colleagues or feel the safety of open spaces again, and what he hopes for is a way to hold the memories without feeling crushed by them, a path back to a life where he can work, speak, and feel a future worth living.
